newsitem.title: FRANCE: France mulls ending winter time change for good.
newsitem.headline: France mulls ending winter time change for good.

text.p: France sets its clocks back one hour to winter time on Sunday, but Prime Minister Alain Juppe believes it may soon be time to scrap the twice-yearly adjustment for good.
Juppe told the daily Sud-Ouest he hoped to reach a formal decision by the end of the year to keep the country year-round on winter time, one hour ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).
In an interview published on Saturday, Juppe said this was closer to solar time than the current summer time, GMT plus two hours, and was therefore more natural for France.
"I hope to be able to decide formally by the end of this year to return to single time," he said.

If this does happen, France would return to summer time next spring and change back to winter time next autumn for good, abandoning the twice-yearly clock changes still in operation in other European Union countries.
Juppe acknowledged that most of France's European partners favoured summertime, which ensures longer light evenings, but said they could not ignore France's position.

French parliamentary reports have recommended year-round winter time, but said France should consult its EU partners first. They warned that Paris would risk a serious row if it were unilaterally to make changes before 1998, when an EU directive on time comes up for review.
France and its EU neighbours now put clocks forward an hour in summer under a policy aimed at saving energy and creating long summer evenings. Clocks in the EU go back to winter time on Sunday.
The French reports argue that energy savings are minimal in summer time and that farmers, truck drivers and children getting up early to go to school would benefit from lighter mornings.
Polls show few French people like the present system.
